branch_hypotheses.alternate_path: Incumbent party recovers enough swing support in marginals to challenge Party C seat lead.
branch_hypotheses.divergence_signal: Sustained improvement in incumbent competitive-riding standing relative to national baseline and more favorable leader evaluations.
branch_hypotheses.trigger: New prime minister delivers credible renewal signals and avoids immediate association with prior fatigue.

branch_hypotheses.alternate_path: Party C wins most seats even without overwhelming popular-vote margin.
branch_hypotheses.divergence_signal: Evidence of strong performance in marginal ridings and reduced opposition vote fragmentation where Party C is competitive.
branch_hypotheses.trigger: Party C converts national polling advantage into geographically efficient support.

branch_hypotheses.alternate_path: Party C leads or remains strong nationally but fails to win the most seats.
branch_hypotheses.divergence_signal: Persistent mismatch between national vote polling and riding/region seat projections.
branch_hypotheses.trigger: Vote distribution remains inefficient for Party C across ridings.

branch_hypotheses.alternate_path: Anti-incumbent vote splits in key ridings, lowering Party C seat conversion.
branch_hypotheses.divergence_signal: Stable local support for minor parties in ridings where Party C needs consolidation to win.
branch_hypotheses.trigger: Other opposition parties retain enough local loyalty to block Party C consolidation.

endpoint_ledger.contradiction_notes: Popular vote plurality alone does not realize this endpoint.
endpoint_ledger.description: Terminal yes endpoint: Party C finishes with more House of Commons seats than every other party.
endpoint_ledger.label: Party C wins most seats

meta.important_question: Will Party C win more House of Commons seats than every other party by election resolution?

endpoint_ledger.rationale: The scenario explicitly resolves yes only on seat plurality, making this the primary terminal condition.
realization_criteria: Official or broadly accepted final seat count shows party_c_seats > incumbent_party_seats and party_c_seats > each_other_party_seat_count.
endpoint_ledger.status_basis: This is the main unresolved forecast endpoint at T0.

endpoint_ledger.contradiction_notes: This endpoint includes cases where Party C wins popular vote but not seat plurality.
endpoint_ledger.description: Terminal no endpoint: another party equals or exceeds Party C in House of Commons seat count by resolution.
endpoint_ledger.label: Party C does not win most seats

meta.important_question: Does the new prime minister materially improve the incumbent party's seat competitiveness during the campaign?

endpoint_ledger.rationale: Source packet explicitly notes that winning popular vote but fewer seats resolves no.
realization_criteria: Official or broadly accepted final seat count shows party_c_seats <= max(other_party_seat_counts).
endpoint_ledger.status_basis: Mutually exclusive alternative to yes remains live at initialization.

endpoint_ledger.contradiction_notes: Reset success alone does not guarantee incumbent wins most seats; it is a mechanism affecting the main endpoint.
endpoint_ledger.description: Intermediate but outcome-relevant endpoint in which the new prime minister measurably improves incumbent electoral position before final vote.
endpoint_ledger.label: Incumbent brand reset succeeds

meta.important_question: Does Party C's support translate efficiently enough across single-member districts to outperform rivals in seat count?

endpoint_ledger.rationale: Needed to preserve the scenario's causal pressure without collapsing it into the final binary endpoint.
realization_criteria: Multiple credible campaign indicators show sustained incumbent improvement versus pre-campaign baseline, especially in seat-competitive ridings or seat projections.
endpoint_ledger.status_basis: Leadership reset is explicitly identified as a key uncertainty shaping final seat outcome.

simulation_brief.core_question: Whether Party C wins more House of Commons seats than every other party in the 2025 Canadian federal election.
simulation_brief.summary: A snap federal election follows a leadership transition in the incumbent governing party. Party C enters with strong national polling history and a clear opposition message, but the incumbent party may regain support under a new leader during the campaign. Electoral outcome depends on seat conversion under single-member districts rather than national vote share alone.
uncertainty_notes: No province-level polling, district maps, or party identities are provided in the corpus.
Leadership effects are directionally ambiguous: renewal versus inherited fatigue.
Seat outcome can diverge materially from popular vote outcome under the electoral system.

sociology_baseline.evidence: Partisan and strategic segments likely update within moderate ideological range during campaign.
Campaign momentum and leader performance can shift turnout enthusiasm without immediate saturation.
Wait-and-see voters may withhold public commitment while privately reassessing.
Election discussion tends to cluster by partisan identity.
Strategic shifts often require multiple reinforcing local signals before voters coordinate.
Core partisan attachment can resist short-run national swing narratives.
Early campaign impressions may fade unless reinforced by ongoing events.

sociology_prompt_influences.description: Single-member districts weaken direct mapping from national vote share to seat plurality.
